body:
## Why
After ~90 minutes of uptime, the loop's claim POST (git/refs) returned 404 on every tick for #61 while a freshly started process succeeded immediately; a manual restart fixed it. The dispatcher's back-off on `unknown` is correct, but backing off forever on a poisoned process state (stale cached baseSha, captured env/credential snapshot — the dead process could not be autopsied) turns a transient into an outage a human has to notice.

## What
- `baseSha` stops being a process-lifetime cache: re-resolve per tick with a conditional request (ETag/304 makes a quiet repo free), so a stale sha can never outlive one tick.
- Track consecutive `unknown` claim results per task in the tick. After 3 consecutive unknown-ticks for the same task: clear every per-process cache (base sha, caps, anything memoized) and log `self-heal: caches dropped`.
- If the claim still returns unknown for 3 more ticks after a cache drop, the loop exits non-zero with a loud final line naming the task and the last error — a dead loop with a reason beats a live loop doing nothing, and lets a supervisor (systemd, the operator, a future watchdog) restart it with fresh state.
- Fake-gh tests: transient 404 → next tick recovers with no restart; persistent 404 → caches dropped at tick 3, exit at tick 6, correct log lines.

## Done when
A claim that starts failing with `unknown` either recovers within a tick of the upstream healing, or the process removes itself with a diagnosable message — never an indefinite silent back-off.
title: A long-lived loop must self-heal from persistent claim failures instead of needing a bounce
